t.3.58.1: Then, after Vārṣṇeya had gone, Puṣkara took from Puṇyaśloka, as he went on gambling, his kingdom and whatever other wealth he had.
t.3.58.2: O king, Puṣkara, laughing, said to Nala, whose kingdom had been taken: "Let the dice game go on once more! What stake do you have left?"
t.3.58.3: Only Damayantī is left to you; everything else has been won by me. Let there be a fine wager of Damayantī, if you think it right.
t.3.58.5: Then the greatly famed Nala, filled with the deepest grief, looked at Puṣkara and stripped the ornaments from all his limbs.
t.3.58.4: When Puṣkara had spoken thus, the heart of Puṇyaśloka seemed to burst with anger, yet he said nothing at all to him.
t.3.58.6: Wearing a single garment, otherwise uncovered, increasing the grief of his friends, the king then went forth, having abandoned his vast royal splendor.
t.3.58.7: Damayantī, clad in a single garment, followed behind him as he went, and the Naiṣadha dwelt with her outside the city for three nights.
t.3.58.8: But Puṣkara, O great king, had it proclaimed in the city: "Whoever treats Nala well shall be put to death by me."
t.3.58.9: But because of Puṣkara's command and his hostility, the townspeople showed him no hospitality, Yudhiṣṭhira.
t.3.58.10: Thus, in the vicinity of the city, the king, though worthy of honor, was not honored; he stayed there three nights, sustaining himself on water alone.
t.3.58.11: But Nala, sorely afflicted by hunger, after many days saw some birds whose wings were like gold.
t.3.58.12: Then the mighty lord of the Niṣadhas thought to himself: "Here is food for me today, and this will also be wealth."
t.3.58.13: Then he covered them with his lower garment, and all of them, taking his garment with them, went off through the sky.
t.3.58.14: But those birds, as they flew up, then spoke words to Nala, seeing him standing on the ground naked, wretched, with his face cast down.
t.3.58.15: We are the dice, O very foolish one, come here wishing to take away your garment, for we had no pleasure while you went off still clothed.
t.3.58.16: Seeing the dice flying off and himself left without clothing, the king of holy renown then spoke to Damayantī.
t.3.58.17: Those through whose wrath I have fallen from sovereignty, O blameless one, and because of whom I, wretched and tormented by hunger, cannot find the means to keep myself alive.
t.3.58.19: I, your husband, have fallen into the utmost adversity, grieving and bereft of my senses; hear these words, which are for your own good.
t.3.58.18: The very dice on whose account the Naiṣadhas withheld their respect from me have now become birds and are carrying off even my garment.
t.3.58.20: These many roads go to the Dakṣiṇāpatha, passing beyond Avantī and the Ṛkṣavant mountain.
t.3.58.21: Here is Vindhya, the great mountain, and the Payoṣṇī, flowing to the sea; and yonder are the hermitages of the great seers, rich with flowers and fruits.
t.3.58.22: This is the road of the Vidarbhas, and this one goes to the Kosalas; and beyond that, in the south, lies this land, the Dakṣiṇāpatha.
t.3.58.23: Then Damayantī, worn down by grief, spoke piteous words to the Naiṣadha in a voice choked with tears.
t.3.58.25: You whose kingdom has been taken and whose wealth has been seized, without a garment, overcome by hunger and weariness, how could I abandon you and go away, leaving you in the desolate forest?
t.3.58.24: My heart trembles and my limbs sink in every part, O king, as I think again and again of your intention.
t.3.58.26: When you are weary and tormented by hunger, brooding upon that former happiness in the dreadful forest, great king, I will dispel your exhaustion.
t.3.58.27: In the opinion of physicians, there is no medicine equal to a wife for all sorrows; this truth I tell you.
t.3.58.28: Nala said: It is just as you have said, Damayantī, O slender-waisted one. For a man in distress there is no friend equal to a wife, and no medicine like her.
t.3.58.30: Damayantī said: If you do not wish to abandon me here, great king, then why is the road to the Vidarbhas being pointed out to me?
t.3.58.29: I have no wish to abandon you; why do you so fearfully suspect it? I would sooner abandon my own self, but never you, O blameless one.
t.3.58.31: And I know, O king, that you ought not to abandon me; but with your mind led astray, you might abandon me, O great lord.
t.3.58.32: For you keep pointing out the road to me again and again, O best of men; for this reason you increase my grief, O you who shine like an immortal.
t.3.58.33: And if this is your intention, O king, that she should go, then let the two of us go together to the Vidarbhas, if you think it right.
t.3.58.34: The king of Vidarbha will honor you there, O giver of honor; honored by him, O king, you will live happily in our house.
